=== claim--curveballs-not-shown-more-stressful-than-fastballs.md
     1	
     2	# A failed attempt to prove that curveballs are more dangerous than fastballs
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig says ASMI had advised for years not to throw curveballs until the growth plates close ("don't throw curve balls until you're old enough to shave") and ran studies to prove it (AgouMNTeyo4 [38:40], [39:11]). The result went the other way:
     5	- Lab: in three biomechanics studies (two in Birmingham, one in Connecticut, some by other groups), elbow torque in a curveball was the same as or a little less than in a fastball (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [39:41]).
     6	- Field: in the 10-year cohort of about 500 youth pitchers, those who started throwing curveballs younger were not the ones who got hurt (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12]).
     7	- Conclusion: "we have not proven that the curve ball is dangerous. We have proven pitching too much is dangerous" (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12], [40:42]).
     8	
     9	In Q&A the speaker is careful: failing to prove danger is not proving safety, so young pitchers should still learn a fastball and a changeup first and add a curveball "when you're ready", because the purpose of off-speed pitches is to disturb the batter's timing (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31], [53:02]). On pitch type, the speaker's group has studied fastballs, curveballs, changeups and sliders: fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful, changeups less so; split-fingered fastballs were not studied (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:02]).
    10	
    11	**Why it works** — Fleisig's measure of stress is elbow torque calculated from motion capture: kinematics (positions and angles) from cameras and kinetics (forces) calculated by equation, torque of about 100 N·m at one arm position shown on screen ("when the arm gets in this position"; the captions do not name the position or the pitch type) (AgouMNTeyo4 [11:46], [12:17], [15:27]). Inference: if torque is the right proxy for ligament load, a pitch with equal torque should carry equal ligament risk; the speaker does not test that proxy in this talk (the speaker says the link from arm stress to injury is unproven, AgouMNTeyo4 [58:38]).
    12	
    13	**When to apply** — As a worked example of a prior belief tested by two designs (lab mechanics and field cohort) and reported when it failed. Also when a coaching rule rests on tradition: ask what the stress measure and the field outcome actually show.
    14	
    15	Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's mission is to help the team "answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones" rather than hand down answers unilaterally (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: Fleisig reversing a position the speaker's own center had held is the posture that mission describes.
    16	
    17	**When NOT to apply** — Baseball pitching in youth to professional levels; the torque comparison does not transfer to any football skill. The speaker does not show the torque numbers for the three curveball studies or the cohort statistics, so the "same or less" result is as stated. "Not proven dangerous" is not "safe", as the speaker says (AgouMNTeyo4 [52:31]). The cohort is the same one that shows the 100-innings result, and the tested pitches did not include the split-finger. A rule about when to introduce a pitch is a coaching and medical decision; do not remove an age guideline on this result alone.
    18	
    19	**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: ASMI's advice before the studies against its results (AgouMNTeyo4 [39:11], [40:42]).
    20	
    21	**Related** — [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (same cohort); [[principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance]] (the 2017 speaker on fastball usage and velocity as risk factors); [[framework--proper-mechanics-as-reference-range-of-healthy-fast-pitchers]].

     3	
     4	**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says defensive three-point percentage, at team or individual level, is "not really a thing", a point he describes as one note the writers of Nylon Calculus have hit many times and which he endorses (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:48], [16:18]), because what happens once the shot leaves the offensive player's hands is "out of the defense's hands". Support: a graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") indicating that individual defensive three-point percentage "looks a lot like a coin flip would look" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:18]). He then qualifies it: he is "not saying that it is just luck", only that it looks like it would if it were (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]). Where defenders do affect a shot:
     5	- Distance: a shooter four feet from the defender on a catch-and-shoot shoots about 34%, at ten feet about 40% (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48], [17:18]).
     6	- Fouls: fouling a jump shooter "turns a 35% shot into a 75 or 80% shot" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18]).
     7	- Late shot clock and end-of-game situations show low three-point percentages "even controlling for all other factors", but he says that style of defense is not available in regular play, because a defender must also stop the drive (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18], [17:48]).
     8	His conclusion: a catch-and-shoot three below roughly 34% is usually not taken, and "even a 34% three is a 51% effective shot", so "defending the three means avoiding the three entirely" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:48], [18:19]). He uses baseball's batting average on balls in play (BABIP) as the analogy, noting that in baseball the "no control" idea was later "relaxed a fair amount" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [15:48]).
     9	
    10	**Why it works** — The speaker gives a partial mechanism: the contest affects the shot through distance, fouls and clock context, and most of the defensive effect shows up as shots not taken (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [18:19]). The coin-flip comparison itself is shown with a graph by another writer and no detail.
    11	
    12	**When to apply** — As a caution against using an outcome rate the defense does not control as a skill metric, and as an example of the risk of reading a flat distribution as "luck". Inference: the same caution applies to any Baylor metric whose variation looks random at the individual level, where one should ask what the measure does not capture before using it to judge a person. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)**
    13	
    14	**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested, not contested: the speaker reconciles the two points himself ("not saying that it is just luck... it looks a lot like it would if it was just luck", BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]) and lists real defender effects (distance, fouls, late clock) alongside. The caption "worth 50% less" at 20 feet at the end of the talk is unclear (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]) and should not be relied on.      2	# In Over 1,000 Plays From One Season, Fewer Than 1% Reached 90% of a Player's Max Speed
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Morris reports that of "over the thousand plays" he broke down from the previous season, "less than 1%" at "any position" reached 90% of that player's max velocity (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). On an average lineman play, travel was 13.5 yards, with direction "25% to the left 25% to the right" (garbled caption: "change direction and art plays 25% to the left"; QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). His conclusion: football is "a game of acceleration" more than of top speed, because a player seldom gets 20 to 30 yards without contact or a change of direction (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). He says this was "shocking" to the head coach and the strength coach, "all about speed" (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). The slide's position breakdown is not captioned, and "the big" is the group he specifies for the 13.5-yard figure ("for our big specifically", QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]).
     5	
     6	**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: short distances, contact and direction changes cut off the chance to build speed (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). Nothing beyond that is given. Inference: because the metric is a percent of each player's own max, a fast player's 90% is a higher absolute speed than a slow player's, so this is a statement about exposure to near-max effort per player, not about absolute mph.
     7	
     8	**When to apply** — When deciding how much of a position's practice or conditioning should be spent at near-max velocity versus accelerating and decelerating. Check it against Baylor's own game files per position group before acting. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary" (Explicit, gap, stated as a gap); Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Inference: Morris's count is about game exposure to near-max speed, whereas the Issurin point is about how long a trained quality persists; they answer different questions and the combination is not tested in this talk.
     9	
    10	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a single program and one season, described by the speaker without a stated method for how 90% of max was computed; the number of plays is only "over a thousand", position and level of play (Kentucky's college offense) are not broken down in the audio. It does not show that max-speed training is unimportant: it shows a low frequency of 90% exposures in games. A player who does reach 90% in a play may still decide that play. The captions run together "90% of their max" with an unclear phrase ("max B"), so treat the exact metric as caption-garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). Inference: the existing Harries return-to-play entries (AFL cases) also use 75-85% and above-90% max-velocity gates, which they call expert opinion, so the 90% cut point here is a convention, not a threshold with evidence.

     1	
     2	# Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):
     5	
     6	1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
     7	2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance". Inference: a placebo test checks for a spurious, method-made effect, not for sampling chance.
     8	3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
     9	4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
    10	5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.
    11	
    12	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.
    13	
    14	**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.
    15	
    16	Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, Eric-authored Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.
    17	
    18	**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.
    19	
    20	**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).

     3	
     4	**What it is** — Eric Eager (introduced as being from Pro Football Focus, PFF) argues that football analytics has three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, player tracking) that are mostly used one at a time, and that they enhance one another when combined (Q3i3FOC-dPE [01:33], [04:12]). The speaker's design, used in three cases: the hand-charted measure is the training target and tracking data supplies the predictors.
     5	- **Pass rush:** charted pressure (and, in a second model, charted win rate) is the label; predictors are play-level context, the defender's position at the snap, charted position labels, and how fast he leaves the ball in the first second, in the vertical direction and as straight-line distance (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:16], [06:47], [07:18]).
     6	- **Linebacker coverage:** the coverage grade is unstable, so the speaker derives a tracking-based trait, play-action "bite distance" (see [[claim--bite-distance-under-expected-is-steadier-than-coverage-grade]]).
     7	- **Receiver deep speed:** speed over the play predicts the PFF grade on go and corner routes (see [[case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown]]).
     8	
     9	PFF charters grade every NFL and college game by hand; the NFL's tracking data comes from chips in the shoulder pads and ball (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:08], [02:40]). The model for pressure is XGBoost, "an ensemble" of decision trees, and returns a per-play pressure probability, not only a yes or no (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:47], [07:48]).
    10	
    11	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning: one measurement of a player's athleticism used forever is "a little bit silly," and expected pressure rate, from tracking data, gives a time-varying measure that tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than the charted data does (Q3i3FOC-dPE [08:49], [09:19], [09:50]). The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: the charted label supplies what counts as success on a play, and tracking supplies how the player moved, so each repairs the other's gap.
    12	
    13	**When to apply** — When one data source labels outcomes but is subjective or coarse, and another measures movement. Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (Explicit, SportSmith article). Inference: this design reuses data already collected, which fits that cost rule. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (Explicit).
    14	
    15	**When NOT to apply** — The slides are not visible and most R-squared values, sample sizes, seasons and play counts are not in the captions (Q3i3FOC-dPE transcript). The speaker works for PFF (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:08]) and presents PFF tools as results; Inference: that is a commercial view. The tracking data the talk uses is the NFL's chip data (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:40]); Inference: a single college program may not hold it. PFF grades come in half-point steps from negative two (caption wording) and graders are not asked to do context math (Q3i3FOC-dPE [26:36], [27:07]). Rated `untested`: the method is described, but each of the three results is oral and qualitative (the only spoken figure, 0.24, is hedged, and the "three or four times" multiple is garbled), and every sibling entry for these results is `untested`; see [[claim--expected-pressure-rate-adds-to-pressure-rate-in-predicting-sacks]].

=== framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers.md
     1	
     2	# A Checklist for Reading Training-Load and Injury Papers
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") opens his research-competition talk with the limits he sees in the published load and injury literature, from soccer and cricket to rugby and Australian football (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Six checks, each with his stated reason:
     5	1. **Contact versus non-contact.** Some papers code injury as a binary, injured in the session or game or not. Then the reader cannot tell whether load had anything to do with it or whether a player rolled up on another's leg (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]).
     6	2. **Time loss versus non-time loss.** Without it, severity is unknown. Time-loss injuries are the ones that keep players out (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:04]).
     7	3. **Censoring.** If an athlete is hurt a quarter of the way into a session and removed, and the model does not censor that session, it can produce "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
     8	4. **Thresholds.** Papers often end with a "train above X load, Y more injuries" rule, but thresholds "bounce around" between papers, even in one sport, because the samples are small, one team and one to two years of data (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).
     9	5. **Team-specific results.** The speaker says these papers are often less about predicting injury for a sport and more about one team and how its coach prepares it, comparing it to inconsistent coffee-and-wine nutrition headlines (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:37]).
    10	6. **Retrospective versus predictive.** Papers say "prediction" in the title, but the model is never tested on unseen data; they are historical accounts of how injuries took place, which, the caption says, "isn't necessarily bad" (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:08]; the caption writes "retro addictive" for retrospective).
    11	
    12	**Why it works** — Each check is paired with the failure it prevents, as listed above. The speaker gives no evidence on how often each failure occurs in the literature; he describes them as "some of the papers" (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Inference: the checks work as a quick screen because each one changes what the reader can conclude (association versus prediction, one team versus a sport).
    13	
    14	**When to apply** — Before acting on a published load-injury result or a vendor claim that load data predicts injury. Eric's baseline: Eric looks at ACWR but does not trust it for anything, calling it "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally," and follows no formal risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this checklist gives specific reasons for that distrust, such as no unseen-data test and unstable thresholds.
    15	
    16	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is one researcher's critique, not a validated appraisal tool, and it gives no scoring or cut-off. It is not a replacement for a formal risk-of-bias instrument. It says nothing about the quality of the speaker's own study beyond what he states; see the case-study entry for that.
    17	
    18	**Example** — The speaker's own, for check 3: an unadjusted model that kicks out "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" because injured athletes' short sessions are left in (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
    19	
    20	**Related** — [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]] (check 6 in practice). [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the speaker's own study handled checks 1 to 3). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]].      1	
     2	# Checking an Outcome-Probability Model: Split by What Happened, Then Calibrate
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Burke's variant 3 predicts complete, incomplete or intercepted for the targeted pass. He checks it two ways (EeBgUCYhezc [15:09], [15:40], [16:12]):
     5	
     6	1. Split plays by what actually happened and read the average predicted completion probability: 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions (targeted passes only, so the numbers look high).
     7	2. A calibration chart for completion probability, which he calls "fairly well calibrated".
     8	
     9	He then reads interceptions with care. The rate is "a low base rate, very very random event" (tipped passes, bobbles, wind), so decision-making is only one factor, and passers vary within "a very tight window" of estimated interception probability (EeBgUCYhezc [17:13], [17:43]). Jameis Winston (name as in captions) had the highest estimated and actual 2018 rate through week 12, but Burke judged most of it came "from inaccurate throws compared to poor decision making" (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]). Two case plays (Winston, and Derek Carr on second and two against what he reads as triple or quadruple coverage) are shown as poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [16:43], [17:13]).
    10	
    11	In Q&A he concedes a class imbalance problem (interceptions are rare) and did not rebalance, because the model does "so many different things all at once" and time was short; he says he did take measures for his earlier Hall of Fame model, "to make sure that the those low rate cases are over represented in the data but not here" (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36], [25:08]).
    12	
    13	**Why it works** — The outcome split is a face-validity check: Inference: a model with signal should give higher completion probability where completions happened. The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: calibration matters when the output will be read as a probability by a coach, because a ranked score can look good while its probabilities are off.
    14	
    15	**When to apply** — Any model whose output a staff member will read as "chance of X". Run both checks before showing it, and say when an outcome is too rare to read (Inference: a handful of interceptions per passer in a season is below what supports a person-level claim).
    16	
    17	Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md; Explicit). Inference: the same logic applies to model outputs; a probability that is not checked is not yet usable.
    18	
    19	**When NOT to apply** — The 79 versus 56 numbers are the speaker's report on one test period; no calibration error value is given (EeBgUCYhezc [16:12]). The interception probabilities are low and the class imbalance was not corrected, so interception results should not drive a decision on a passer (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36]). The decision-versus-accuracy split for Winston is an assertion without a measured breakdown in the talk.
    20	
    21	**Example** — The speaker's: the 2018 Winston interception rate, assigned mostly to inaccurate throws, not poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]).

=== framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting.md
     1	
     2	# Expected Points Saved: Tackle as Treatment, EPA as Outcome, Propensity Weighting
     3	
     4	**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames defender credit as a treatment effect (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02]).
     5	- **Treatment:** a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle on the play.
     6	- **Outcome:** expected points added (EPA), the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits.
     7	- **Expected points saved (EPS):** expected EPA on the play if the defender did not make the tackle, minus expected EPA if he did (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02], [04:33]).
     8	- **Architecture:** a transformer that processes all 22 players at once; the speaker says its attention mechanism captures defender coordination and interference effects (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33]).
     9	- **Inputs (shown on a causal graph, DAG):** each defender's x-y position, speed and direction; the same for the ball carrier; relational features (defender relative to ball carrier); the 10 teammates of each defender; opponents; game context (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33], [05:04]).
    10	- **Two models:** a propensity score model (probability a defender makes a tackle given all tracking information) and an outcome model (expected EPA with and without that defender's tackle) (JHgeEo3n1do [05:04], [05:35]).
    11	- **Weighting:** inverse propensity weighting to build a "pseudo population" in which tackle involvement is independent of context and "effectively randomized" (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]).
    12	- **Doubly robust estimation:** named at the close as protection "against model misspecification" (JHgeEo3n1do [09:41]).
    13	
    14	**Why it works** — The speaker's stated logic is that reweighting by the inverse of the probability of being involved removes the context that made involvement likely (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]), and a low-probability defender who makes a tackle gets higher weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). He gives no proof or diagnostic that the propensity model balances the groups. Inference: the estimate is only as good as the propensity model, which the talk does not show being checked.
    15	
    16	**When to apply** — As a recipe for any "who deserves credit" question where several people act on one outcome: define the treatment, define the outcome, model who gets the treatment, then reweight. Eric's baseline: none found. method-baseline.md holds no position on causal inference or counterfactual models. Inference: Baylor lacks league-wide tracking data for this exact build, so the lasting use is the design logic (treatment, outcome, propensity, weighting) when judging an outside metric someone brings to Applied Performance.
    17	
    18	**When NOT to apply** — The speaker calls it a proof of concept on the first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). The captions do not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model was checked, or how the "treatment" is defined for players who get credit without tackling (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The video description names adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty and sensitivity analyses, but none is described in the talk (JHgeEo3n1do meta.json description, not in the talk). A questioner points out that scheme and assignment are not in the data, and the speaker says it is ongoing research (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:13], [12:43]). `untested`: the captions give few validation values (about 41 percent of variance in tackle-play outcomes explained at team level, [08:10]; higher R-squared and lower RMSE than supervised models, with no values captioned, [08:40]); no check of the propensity model is described.
    19	
    20	**Example** — The speaker's example play: the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].
    21	
    22	**Related** — [[principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation]], [[framework--validating-a-causal-metric-with-no-ground-truth]], [[claim--defender-interference-in-68-percent-of-plays]], [[claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting]]. His conclusion: football is "a game of acceleration" more than of top speed, because a player seldom gets 20 to 30 yards without contact or a change of direction (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). He says this was "shocking" to the head coach and the strength coach, "all about speed" (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). The slide's position breakdown is not captioned, and "the big" is the group he specifies for the 13.5-yard figure ("for our big specifically", QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]).
     5	
     6	**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker: short distances, contact and direction changes cut off the chance to build speed (QLdbKUiNadg [11:52]). Nothing beyond that is given. Inference: because the metric is a percent of each player's own max, a fast player's 90% is a higher absolute speed than a slow player's, so this is a statement about exposure to near-max effort per player, not about absolute mph.
     7	
     8	**When to apply** — When deciding how much of a position's practice or conditioning should be spent at near-max velocity versus accelerating and decelerating. Check it against Baylor's own game files per position group before acting. Eric's baseline: "No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary" (Explicit, gap, stated as a gap); Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." (Explicit, interview-confirmed). Inference: Morris's count is about game exposure to near-max speed, whereas the Issurin point is about how long a trained quality persists; they answer different questions and the combination is not tested in this talk.

It does not show that max-speed training is unimportant: it shows a low frequency of 90% exposures in games. A player who does reach 90% in a play may still decide that play. The captions run together "90% of their max" with an unclear phrase ("max B"), so treat the exact metric as caption-garbled (QLdbKUiNadg [11:21]). Inference: the existing Harries return-to-play entries (AFL cases) also use 75-85% and above-90% max-velocity gates, which they call expert opinion, so the 90% cut point here is a convention, not a threshold with evidence.

     5	- **Individual skill development:** players working more on long-distance shooting because the three "is a vital piece to getting playing time" and staying in the league.

     7	- **Downsizing:** less time with two traditional big men and more shooters on the floor.

    11	**Why it works** — The speaker gives these as his theory and does not test any one cause. Inference: with four causes named together and no attribution among them, the account cannot say which one mattered most.

     1	
     2	# Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):
     5	
     6	1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
     7	2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance". Inference: a placebo test checks for a spurious, method-made effect, not for sampling chance.
     8	3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
     9	4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
    10	5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.
    11	
    12	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.
    13	
    14	**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.
    15	
    16	Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, Eric-authored Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.
    17	
    18	**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.
    19	
    20	**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).
    21	
    22	**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; calibration of a different model: [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]] and [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]].

     2	# Charted Grades as Labels, Tracking Data as Predictors
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Eric Eager (introduced as being from Pro Football Focus, PFF) argues that football analytics has three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, player tracking) that are mostly used one at a time, and that they enhance one another when combined (Q3i3FOC-dPE [01:33], [04:12]). The speaker's design, used in three cases: the hand-charted measure is the training target and tracking data supplies the predictors.
     5	- **Pass rush:** charted pressure (and, in a second model, charted win rate) is the label; predictors are play-level context, the defender's position at the snap, charted position labels, and how fast he leaves the ball in the first second, in the vertical direction and as straight-line distance (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:16], [06:47], [07:18]).
     6	- **Linebacker coverage:** the coverage grade is unstable, so the speaker derives a tracking-based trait, play-action "bite distance" (see [[claim--bite-distance-under-expected-is-steadier-than-coverage-grade]]).
     7	- **Receiver deep speed:** speed over the play predicts the PFF grade on go and corner routes (see [[case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown]]).
     8	
     9	PFF charters grade every NFL and college game by hand; the NFL's tracking data comes from chips in the shoulder pads and ball (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:08], [02:40]). The model for pressure is XGBoost, "an ensemble" of decision trees, and returns a per-play pressure probability, not only a yes or no (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:47], [07:48]).
    10	
    11	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning: one measurement of a player's athleticism used forever is "a little bit silly," and expected pressure rate, from tracking data, gives a time-varying measure that tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than the charted data does (Q3i3FOC-dPE [08:49], [09:19], [09:50]). The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: the charted label supplies what counts as success on a play, and tracking supplies how the player moved, so each repairs the other's gap.
    12	
    13	**When to apply** — When one data source labels outcomes but is subjective or coarse, and another measures movement. Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (Explicit, SportSmith article). Inference: this design reuses data already collected, which fits that cost rule. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (Explicit).
    14	
    15	**When NOT to apply** — The slides are not visible and most R-squared values, sample sizes, seasons and play counts are not in the captions (Q3i3FOC-dPE transcript). The speaker works for PFF (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:08]) and presents PFF tools as results; Inference: that is a commercial view. The tracking data the talk uses is the NFL's chip data (Q3i3FOC-dPE [02:40]); Inference: a single college program may not hold it. PFF grades come in half-point steps from negative two (caption wording) and graders are not asked to do context math (Q3i3FOC-dPE [26:36], [27:07]). Rated `untested`: the method is described, but each of the three results is oral and qualitative (the only spoken figure, 0.24, is hedged, and the "three or four times" multiple is garbled), and every sibling entry for these results is `untested`; see [[claim--expected-pressure-rate-adds-to-pressure-rate-in-predicting-sacks]].
    16	
    17	**Example** — The speaker's pass-rush case: the vertical distance covered in the first second is the most important variable for a pressure (Q3i3FOC-dPE [06:47]).

=== framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers.md
     1	
     2	# A Checklist for Reading Training-Load and Injury Papers
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") opens his research-competition talk with the limits he sees in the published load and injury literature, from soccer and cricket to rugby and Australian football (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Six checks, each with his stated reason:
     5	1. **Contact versus non-contact.** Some papers code injury as a binary, injured in the session or game or not. Then the reader cannot tell whether load had anything to do with it or whether a player rolled up on another's leg (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]).
     6	2. **Time loss versus non-time loss.** Without it, severity is unknown. Time-loss injuries are the ones that keep players out (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:04]).
     7	3. **Censoring.** If an athlete is hurt a quarter of the way into a session and removed, and the model does not censor that session, it can produce "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
     8	4. **Thresholds.** Papers often end with a "train above X load, Y more injuries" rule, but thresholds "bounce around" between papers, even in one sport, because the samples are small, one team and one to two years of data (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).
     9	5. **Team-specific results.** The speaker says these papers are often less about predicting injury for a sport and more about one team and how its coach prepares it, comparing it to inconsistent coffee-and-wine nutrition headlines (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:37]).
    10	6. **Retrospective versus predictive.** Papers say "prediction" in the title, but the model is never tested on unseen data; they are historical accounts of how injuries took place, which, the caption says, "isn't necessarily bad" (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:08]; the caption writes "retro addictive" for retrospective).
    11	
    12	**Why it works** — Each check is paired with the failure it prevents, as listed above. The speaker gives no evidence on how often each failure occurs in the literature; he describes them as "some of the papers" (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Inference: the checks work as a quick screen because each one changes what the reader can conclude (association versus prediction, one team versus a sport).
    13	
    14	**When to apply** — Before acting on a published load-injury result or a vendor claim that load data predicts injury. Eric's baseline: Eric looks at ACWR but does not trust it for anything, calling it "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally," and follows no formal risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this checklist gives specific reasons for that distrust, such as no unseen-data test and unstable thresholds.
    15	
    16	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is one researcher's critique, not a validated appraisal tool, and it gives no scoring or cut-off. It is not a replacement for a formal risk-of-bias instrument. It says nothing about the quality of the speaker's own study beyond what he states; see the case-study entry for that.
    17	
    18	**Example** — The speaker's own, for check 3: an unadjusted model that kicks out "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" because injured athletes' short sessions are left in (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
    19	
    20	**Related** — [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]] (check 6 in practice). [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the speaker's own study handled checks 1 to 3). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestions (not compared in this batch): [[impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]], [[griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]].

     2	# Checking an Outcome-Probability Model: Split by What Happened, Then Calibrate
     3	
     4	**What it is** — Burke's variant 3 predicts complete, incomplete or intercepted for the targeted pass. He checks it two ways (EeBgUCYhezc [15:09], [15:40], [16:12]):
     5	
     6	1. Split plays by what actually happened and read the average predicted completion probability: 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions (targeted passes only, so the numbers look high).
     7	2. A calibration chart for completion probability, which he calls "fairly well calibrated".
     8	
     9	He then reads interceptions with care. The rate is "a low base rate, very very random event" (tipped passes, bobbles, wind), so decision-making is only one factor, and passers vary within "a very tight window" of estimated interception probability (EeBgUCYhezc [17:13], [17:43]). Jameis Winston (name as in captions) had the highest estimated and actual 2018 rate through week 12, but Burke judged most of it came "from inaccurate throws compared to poor decision making" (EeBgUCYhezc [17:43]). Two case plays (Winston, and Derek Carr on second and two against what he reads as triple or quadruple coverage) are shown as poor decisions (EeBgUCYhezc [16:43], [17:13]).
    10	
    11	In Q&A he concedes a class imbalance problem (interceptions are rare) and did not rebalance, because the model does "so many different things all at once" and time was short; he says he did take measures for his earlier Hall of Fame model, "to make sure that the those low rate cases are over represented in the data but not here" (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36], [25:08]).
    12	
    13	**Why it works** — The outcome split is a face-validity check: Inference: a model with signal should give higher completion probability where completions happened. The speaker gives no further mechanism. Inference: calibration matters when the output will be read as a probability by a coach, because a ranked score can look good while its probabilities are off.
    14	
    15	**When to apply** — Any model whose output a staff member will read as "chance of X". Run both checks before showing it, and say when an outcome is too rare to read (Inference: a handful of interceptions per passer in a season is below what supports a person-level claim).
    16	
    17	Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md; Explicit). Inference: the same logic applies to model outputs; a probability that is not checked is not yet usable.
    18	
    19	**When NOT to apply** — The 79 versus 56 numbers are the speaker's report on one test period; no calibration error value is given (EeBgUCYhezc [16:12]). The interception probabilities are low and the class imbalance was not corrected, so interception results should not drive a decision on a passer (EeBgUCYhezc [24:36]). The decision-versus-accuracy split for Winston is an assertion without a measured breakdown in the talk.

=== framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting.md
     1	
     2	# Expected Points Saved: Tackle as Treatment, EPA as Outcome, Propensity Weighting
     3	
     4	**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames defender credit as a treatment effect (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02]).
     5	- **Treatment:** a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle on the play.
     6	- **Outcome:** expected points added (EPA), the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits.
     7	- **Expected points saved (EPS):** expected EPA on the play if the defender did not make the tackle, minus expected EPA if he did (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02], [04:33]).
     8	- **Architecture:** a transformer that processes all 22 players at once; the speaker says its attention mechanism captures defender coordination and interference effects (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33]).
     9	- **Inputs (shown on a causal graph, DAG):** each defender's x-y position, speed and direction; the same for the ball carrier; relational features (defender relative to ball carrier); the 10 teammates of each defender; opponents; game context (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33], [05:04]).
    10	- **Two models:** a propensity score model (probability a defender makes a tackle given all tracking information) and an outcome model (expected EPA with and without that defender's tackle) (JHgeEo3n1do [05:04], [05:35]).
    11	- **Weighting:** inverse propensity weighting to build a "pseudo population" in which tackle involvement is independent of context and "effectively randomized" (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]).
    12	- **Doubly robust estimation:** named at the close as protection "against model misspecification" (JHgeEo3n1do [09:41]).
    13	
    14	**Why it works** — The speaker's stated logic is that reweighting by the inverse of the probability of being involved removes the context that made involvement likely (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]), and a low-probability defender who makes a tackle gets higher weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). He gives no proof or diagnostic that the propensity model balances the groups. Inference: the estimate is only as good as the propensity model, which the talk does not show being checked.
    15	
    16	**When to apply** — As a recipe for any "who deserves credit" question where several people act on one outcome: define the treatment, define the outcome, model who gets the treatment, then reweight. Eric's baseline: none found. method-baseline.md holds no position on causal inference or counterfactual models. Inference: Baylor lacks league-wide tracking data for this exact build, so the lasting use is the design logic (treatment, outcome, propensity, weighting) when judging an outside metric someone brings to Applied Performance.
    17	
    18	**When NOT to apply** — The speaker calls it a proof of concept on the first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). The captions do not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model was checked, or how the "treatment" is defined for players who get credit without tackling (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The video description names adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty and sensitivity analyses, but none is described in the talk (JHgeEo3n1do meta.json description, not in the talk). A questioner points out that scheme and assignment are not in the data, and the speaker says it is ongoing research (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:13], [12:43]). `untested`: the captions give few validation values (about 41 percent of variance in tackle-play outcomes explained at team level, [08:10]; higher R-squared and lower RMSE than supervised models, with no values captioned, [08:40]); no check of the propensity model is described.
    19	
    20	**Example** — The speaker's example play: the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].
    21	
    22	**Related** — [[principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation]], [[framework--validating-a-causal-metric-with-no-ground-truth]], [[claim--defender-interference-in-68-percent-of-plays]], [[claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting]].
